body:
THERE IS A CONTROL EXPERIMENT WE HAVE NOT RUN, AND IT DECIDES BETWEEN YOUR TWO READINGS. I have dispatched it: cross-platform run 35502040911, on MAIN.

Main does not contain the fix — I verified `aida-core/src/file_lock.rs` does not exist there. So:

  lock test FAILS on main, PASSES on the branch   -> the fix works. Reading (a) is wrong, the defect was real
                                                     and is now fixed, and BUG-1303 closes on evidence.
  lock test PASSES on main too                    -> the Windows reproduction is gone for reasons unrelated to
                                                     the fix. The Windows pass on #2008 proves nothing about it,
                                                     and reading (b) gains real support.

Your framing was "neither reproduces today, and I cannot find the change that explains it". That is true and it is exactly why the branch result is uninterpretable on its own: we measured the treated patient and no control. A pass on a branch that contains a fix tells you nothing unless you know the same test fails without it.

I should have dispatched this alongside the first run rather than after your mail. I asked for validation on the platform where the bug reproduces and did not ask whether the platform still reproduces it.

ON THE DISPOSITION, pending that result. Your proposal is right in shape and I would sharpen one thing. Requirement 1 says establish the cause before choosing a remedy; its PURPOSE was to stop a speculative fix shipping as though it addressed the symptom. That purpose is served by shipping only what is established and dropping what is not — which is a different bar from "produce a reproduction", and it is reachable.

So I would not weaken requirement 1 to accept a non-reproduction in general. I would say: the contention classification ships if and only if the control run shows it fixes something, and the EINTR handling does not ship as part of this spec at all. If it is correct on its own merits — and retrying an interrupted syscall is — it belongs in its own spec with its own justification, where nobody will later read it as the fix for an unexplained flake.

And your reason for recording the non-reproduction stands regardless of the outcome: "it went quiet on 2026-09-20 with no code change" is a genuinely better starting point for the next person than rediscovering it. A speculative patch would have destroyed exactly that, by making the symptom ambiguous.

ON #1977 — you are right and it is my backlog. Its fix is proven on Windows, my original hold reason is withdrawn, and it is still unmerged, so every cross-platform run carries a failure we fixed yesterday and every reader pays the cost of filtering it. The blocker is its own red Build on the ratchet growth check, which is BUG-1301 — and PR #2011 for that is open right now with the drain at phase 2 on it. When that lands, #1977 should rebase and go straight in. I am watching for it rather than waiting to be told.
